tur63-5: How long is a boot worn after a broken ankle, when does the swelling go down and when can you drive? Tips to support recovery, warning signs and six home exercises.
tur63-6: Has your ankle been broken, and are you now walking in a boot or cast? Stable fractures of the thin bone on the outside of the ankle (the fibula) almost always heal without surgery. The bone usually heals in 6–12 weeks, and that is when the real work starts: getting back the movement, strength and balance of your ankle. This guide covers the exercises you can do at home during and after the boot or cast stage.
tur63-7: Raise your foot when resting and build up the time you spend on your feet gradually. If you need a painkiller, ask your doctor which one is right for you.
tur63-8: If you are being treated in a boot, the first three exercises start straight away once your team allows; if you are in a cast, they start after the cast is removed. The last three are usually added after week 6. Mild discomfort is normal but should settle within 2 hours.
tur63-9: It depends on the type of fracture. For stable outer ankle fractures, a boot is usually worn when on your feet for 1 to 4 weeks, and the boot and crutches are stopped by week 6 at the latest. For fractures treated in a cast, this is often 6 weeks. In a randomised trial in Finland, 3 weeks in a cast or brace for stable outer ankle fractures gave results as good as the usual 6 weeks in a cast.
tur63-10: Do not drive in a boot or cast. You can start once you have stopped using the boot, can walk normally and can do an emergency stop safely; try it somewhere quiet first. If the fracture is in your left ankle and you drive an automatic, it may be possible to start sooner once the boot or cast is off; check this with your team.

tur63-17: The power of hugs: 404 healthy adults were phoned on 14 evenings and asked about that day's conflicts and hugs, and were then exposed to a common cold virus. In those with strong social support and those who hugged more often, the rise in infection risk linked to conflict was weaker; among those who fell ill, these people also had milder symptoms. This is an observational study; it does not show that hugging protects on its own.
